The first one, I think, is one of the most exciting techniques out there is speculative decoding. So, as you might know, usually an LLM
generates one token at a time and then generates another token. So, it's an auto-regressive process. Now, the idea is of speculative decoding is, "Wait, can we not generate more than
one token at a time?" And this actually works by using a so-called draft model. So, this draft model will generate, for instance, in this example, we have the
prompt, "Paris is a" and then our draft model will generate beautiful and historic European. And then our original target model will verify what this small
draft had or draft model has generated and say, "Oh, yeah, I would have also generated beautiful and I would also generated the word end,
but with historic, I don't agree with the word historic. I would have said and predicted vibrant, right?" But now we have with one forward pass,
we have generated three tokens instead of one token because verifying tokens is computationally way cheaper than generating them. So, speculative decoding is a very, very
nice technique to speed up the inter-token latency significantly. Either you can train your own head or certain models, open-source models, come with speculative decoding heads
pre-trained for you. So, if you find such a model, uh or if you use an open-source model, Google if it's a supporting speculative decoding and make sure if it is that you
actually enable it because that's really a nice technique. Another more advanced technique I want to present to you is disaggregated inference. So, disaggregated inference
covers the problem that the prefill phase and the decode phase, so the time to first token and the inter-token latency are not optimizing the same thing. As I
mentioned in the beginning, one is compute bound, one is memory bound. And if you really want to optimize those two things, you might want to split them up
so you can fully optimize for something that is compute bound and fully optimize for something that is memory bound. And that's the idea of disaggregated
inference. You have separate prefill workers and decode workers and you send the KV cache between them. Now, the prefill workers predict the first token
while the decode workers will predict the remaining tokens. This technique is super advanced, so I would apply it to like very high volume traffic scenarios
